questions.prompt: Why do GPUs group 32 threads into a warp that issues one instruction at a time?
options: To pay for instruction fetch, decode and scheduling once per 32 threads
Because DRAM returns 32 bytes at a time
questions.explanation: Sharing one instruction stream across 32 lanes amortises the control logic, leaving more area for arithmetic and registers.

questions.prompt: You launch a kernel over n = 5,000 elements with blocks of 128 threads, one element per thread. How many blocks do you need?
questions.explanation: ⌈5000 / 128⌉ = ⌈39.06⌉ = 40 blocks (5,120 threads; the last 120 do nothing because of the guard).

questions.prompt: A GPU has 10 SMs and each SM can hold 3 of your blocks at once. Your grid has 70 blocks. How many waves does it take (assuming all blocks take equal time)?
questions.explanation: 30 blocks run at once; ⌈70 / 30⌉ = 3 waves, and the last wave only uses 10 of the 30 slots.

questions.prompt: In c[i] = a[i] + b[i] with i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, what is thread 5 of block 3 responsible for when blocks have 256 threads?

options: All threads of a block run on the same SM
Blocks of a grid may run in any order
A block can be split across two SMs if it's large
Threads in the same block can cooperate through shared memory
questions.explanation: A block is the unit placed on one SM. It can use that SM's shared memory, and blocks are independent and unordered.

questions.prompt: Why does the vector-add kernel need if (i < n)?
options: Because the grid is rounded up to whole blocks, so some threads have no element
To make the memory accesses coalesced
It doesn't; it's only for readability
questions.explanation: Blocks have a fixed size, so the grid covers ⌈n/block⌉ × block threads and the extras must not touch memory.
